questions.q: Define 'ritual dimension' and 'secular dimension' of caste in contemporary India, giving one example of each.
questions.a: Ritual dimension: practices governed by purity-pollution rules — e.g., endogamous marriage, restrictions on commensality (who one eats with), temple entry, death rituals. Secular dimension: spheres where caste operates through material interests — e.g., electoral vote banks, recruitment networks in factories, access to reservation benefits, land ownership patterns. A wrong answer that lists only ritual practices (or only economic ones) reveals the student sees caste as either purely religious or purely economic, missing the NCERT's core argument that both coexist and interact.

questions.q: The NCERT states: "For the upper caste urban middle classes, caste has become invisible... For the scheduled castes and tribes, caste has become all too visible." Explain this paradox in your own words using the concepts of 'inherited educational capital' and 'collective assets'.
questions.a: Upper castes accumulated educational/economic capital over generations when caste barriers gave them exclusive access to schools and public-sector jobs; by the third generation, their success appears meritocratic, making caste seem irrelevant in public life (though it persists in marriage). SC/ST/OBC groups lack that inherited capital, face ongoing discrimination, and rely on caste identity as a collective asset to claim reservation — the only institutional lifeline available — which forces their caste into the spotlight. A wrong answer that blames 'reservation alone' for making caste visible ignores the structural disadvantage that makes reservation necessary.

questions.q: A factory in 1970s Mumbai recruits workers through a mukadam (labour contractor) from his own village and jati. In 2024, the same factory hires through an online portal and campus placements. Using the concepts of 'caste-based recruitment networks' and 'modern industry creating jobs with no caste rules', explain what has changed and what persists.
questions.a: Changed: formal recruitment replaces kinship/jati networks; new jobs (IT, engineering) have no prescribed caste occupation. Persists: informal referrals still favour existing employees' caste networks; prejudice against Dalits continues in hiring for 'clean' vs 'dirty' jobs; dominant castes (e.g., Marathas in Maharashtra) use political clout to secure local quotas. A wrong answer claiming 'caste has disappeared from factories' misses the NCERT evidence that mill recruitment remained caste-segmented long after Independence.

questions.q: Compare M.N. Srinivas's concepts of 'Sanskritisation' and 'Dominant Caste'. How do they explain different trajectories of caste mobility in post-Independence India?
questions.a: Sanskritisation: lower/middle castes adopt rituals (vegetarianism, teetotalism, Brahmin priests) of higher castes to claim ritual status — symbolic, cultural mobility without structural change. Dominant Caste: intermediate castes (Yadavs, Vokkaligas, Marathas) gain economic/political power through land reforms + demographic strength + adult franchise — material, structural mobility that reshapes regional power. A wrong answer that conflates them (e.g., saying dominant castes Sanskritise) misses that dominant castes often assert their own identity rather than imitate Brahmins.

questions.q: Critique the statement: "If the state operates in a caste-blind manner, caste inequality will automatically disappear." Use evidence from the NCERT on government jobs, education, and reservation.
questions.a: The statement is false. Caste-blind recruitment in early decades pitted educated upper castes against illiterate lower castes on 'equal terms', reproducing advantage. Subsidised professional education (IITs, medical colleges) benefited upper castes who already had school access. Reservation — the only non-caste-blind policy — created pathways for SC/ST/OBC but also made caste a visible political category. A wrong answer agreeing with the statement ignores the NCERT's explicit argument that formal equality ≠ substantive equality when starting points are unequal.

questions.q: Design a 5-question survey to test whether caste operates more in the ritual or secular sphere among your classmates. Justify each question's placement.
questions.a: Example questions: (1) "Would your family accept a marriage partner from a different jati?" (Ritual — endogamy). (2) "Do you know the caste of your closest friends?" (Ritual — social networks). (3) "Have you ever benefited from caste-based reservation in admission/jobs?" (Secular — policy access). (4) "Are caste-based voting appeals common in your area?" (Secular — politics). (5) "Do you follow any food-sharing rules based on caste at home?" (Ritual — commensality). A poor survey asks only about reservation or only about marriage, failing to capture the dual dimensions.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Caste in contemporary India refers to the persistence of the traditional varna-jati hierarchy in ritual domains (endogamy, purity-pollution rules, commensality) alongside its ______ in secular spheres (occupational mobility, political mobilisation, educational access) due to constitutional provisions, market forces, urbanisation, and democratic politics.

Fill in the blank: Imagine a 22-year-old ______ graduate from a traditional Brahmin family in Bengaluru who eats in the office cafeteria with colleagues of all backgrounds, dates a non-Brahmin classmate, yet insists on a Brahmin priest for his wedding and prefers a spouse from his own jati.
What is Caste in contemporary India? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: Caste in contemporary India refers to the persistence of the traditional varna-jati hierarchy in ritual domains (endogamy, purity-pollution rules, commensality) alongside its transformation in secular spheres (occupational mobility, political mobilisation, educational access) due to constitutional provisions, market forces, urbanisation.

questions.q: What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Caste in contemporary India?
questions.a: Students often think 'caste is weakening everywhere' because they see intercaste dining in colleges or upper-caste peers saying 'caste doesn't matter'.

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can (1) distinguish between ritual and secular dimensions of caste with concrete examples, (2) explain why caste has become 'invisible' for urban upper castes but hyper-visible for SC/ST/OBC groups, and (3) evaluate the paradox that protective discrimination policies simultaneously weaken caste-based economic monopolies and.
